Who handles this key?

The old application decides with branches. Ochazuke resolves a binding, then runs a named operation. Read the actual code, one version at a time.

Old way / application-owned routing

One handler knows every context.

Search mode, detail editing, page overrides and action execution meet in the same function. Adding behavior can mean another condition and another precedence decision.

Search owns typingThe search branch returns before the rest of the handler.
Pages intercept keysPanes, reviews and queue branch before the main action switch.
“Open” branches againDesk, projects, settings and row kinds each change what open means.

The large switch lives in action execution

Gmtm's exec is 196 lines. Keys, the palette and help share it. It switches on action IDs, not physical keys. Ochazuke instead registers each operation with its handler.

This is not “no keymaps” versus “keymaps.” Both older apps already have action registries and binding mechanisms. Matomeru-old still has a large routing function. Gmtm has a shorter router-based handler, but its app still chooses the active context in code.

New way / shared resolution, declared behavior

Bind the key. Define the action.

The application declares mode tables and named operations. Ochazuke's shared runtime handles dispatch. These are current ochazuke APIs, not evidence that matomeru-old or gmtm has already migrated.

The basic idea

Look up the key in the current mode's table, fall back to its key class, then to the catch-all. Run the selected action with the key and state. This captures the essence of the approach: bindings are data, and dispatch is a shared lookup.

This simplified model assumes an any fallback exists. Ochazuke adds context traversal, guards, inherited tables and multi-key state; its binding rows hold named operation requests rather than direct callbacks. The groups below describe those extensions, and the Go excerpts show their implementation.

What extends the basic lookup

The simple expression assumes one active table, one key per binding, one class per key, and a handler stored directly in the binding. These six mechanisms explain the extra resolver code. Expand one to see the detailed support and related tooling.

Focus stackLook through focused instance, parent contexts, and app bindings.
SupportBehavior and example
Noun and instance bindingsDeclare behavior for every instance of a noun, or override one specific instance. At a given context level, instance rows precede noun rows.
Inner-to-outer bubblingThe focused context gets the first ordinary binding match, then its parents and the app. A CSV cell can bind i while its row binds d d. See the focus stack.
Modal boundariesAn active modal restricts the context walk. Bindings from the page beneath it do not accidentally answer; modal and app bindings still participate.
Live help and footer hintsHelp and hints derive from the binding tables. Help groups rows by binding-owner noun, inner to outer, with movement last; scrolling keeps the current owner heading visible.
Capture bindingsLet outer bindings answer before inner contexts.
SupportBehavior and example
Outer-to-inner captureCaptured() bindings resolve before ordinary bindings. The default app quit binding can answer before an inner terminal's any row swallows the key.
Terminal passthroughA passthrough base mode skips capture. The terminal's rows receive keys such as ctrl+c; a leader binding provides commands such as detach.
Mode inheritanceRead the active mode's table, then inherited tables.
SupportBehavior and example
Mode-specific and any-mode tablesBind different behavior in normal, insert, visual or application-defined modes. The empty mode table supplies any-mode rows when resolution is not exclusive.
Mode inheritanceExtends reads a parent table after the child's rows. A specialized selection mode can reuse another mode's bindings without copying them. See Noun.tables.
Key sequencesFor g g, retain the first key and wait. If g also has a binding, keep it as a timeout fallback.
SupportBehavior and example
Multi-key sequencesDeclare g g, d d or t u as binding data. The runtime tracks prefixes rather than requiring a key-specific branch in the app.
Ambiguous-prefix timeoutIf both g and g g exist, wait for a continuation and retain the completed match as a fallback. BindingTimeout controls the wait; stale timeout messages are ignored.
Sequence cancellation and mismatchGenerated bindings such as g esc cancel a prefix. A mismatch leaves the prefix, runs a stored completed match if present, then offers the new key fresh to the stack.
Exclusive pending modesOperator, count, register, macro and sequence states can temporarily own input. Pending rows run without unrelated base-mode bindings intercepting the next key.
Counts and operator payloadsPending state carries typed values such as count, operator and operator count. Built-in editor tables use them for commands such as 3j and dw.
Re-dispatch and one-shot cleanupPending modes normally return to their previous mode when consumed. A row's replay flag can offer the key again after its request runs. See runRow.
Paste eventsPaste carries a separate event flag and matches paste patterns rather than being interpreted as a sequence of command keys.
Macro recording and replayMacro modes record keys and paste events, then replay them through the same dispatch path. Recording uses a shadow mode so ordinary input behavior still runs.
Guards and patternsSkip inapplicable rows; rank matching key classes.
SupportBehavior and example
Exact keys and aliasesMap a named key to a request. Several keys can invoke the same operation, such as i and enter calling cell.edit.
Key classes and catch-allsMatch digit, alpha, printable, paste or any. Patterns can exclude keys, such as digit-0, or name a set, such as one-of:h j k l. Exact keys rank before class matches. See lookup.
Conditional applicabilityA binding's when names a guard. Operations can also have applicability guards, so an unavailable operation is rejected by keyboard, palette, CLI and API alike.
Binding validationValidateBindings checks row shapes, modes, guards, operations, argument names and argument sources before an application runs its tables.
Named operationsA binding produces a request. Execution resolves its handler, including scoped overrides.
SupportBehavior and example
Named, atomic operationsA binding contains a request such as app.pin, not an inline key callback. Verb registers its handler. The same operation can run through Execute, the palette or the CLI.
Scoped action overridesAction("selection.inspect", handler) gives an existing operation a context-specific handler. The nearest applicable noun override wins; otherwise the operation's default handler runs. See ActionFor.
Arguments and matched targetsRequests accept literal arguments. FromKey, FromPayload and Join fill values from input or pending state. A row-owned operation can target the row even while a child cell has focus.
Confirmation and errorsExecution validates arguments and targets, checks applicability, and can open an operation's confirmation prompt. The model reports dispatch errors in its status line. See execution.
Editor operations and registersThe shared editor's binding tables expose Vim-style and Readline editing, visual selections, undo/redo, yank/paste and named registers. These are registered operations, not special cases in the resolver.
Action history and repeatOperation execution records history. The framework's repeat operation can replay eligible changes through the same operation system.
JSON binding configurationGo declarations and JSON use the same binding-row shape. bindings load and Runtime.Bind install rows; matching overrides replace defaults and null requests unbind them. Referenced operations, guards, instances and modes must exist.
Active binding inspectionbindings list reports bindings for the current focus and mode, including pending states. It respects shadowing and operation applicability rather than dumping every table.
All-table JSON exportbindings list --all returns every stored noun and instance binding row across all modes in deterministic table order. For CSV, run go run ./examples/csv bindings list --all. This exports rows, not handler implementations or mode inheritance declarations.
Descriptions and argument previewsOperation descriptions, per-binding hint/help, and footer hiding control discovery. Help previews resolved arguments and leaves future pattern-key values explicit.

Without these requirements, the basic lookup is enough. Ochazuke trades a large application-specific keyboard handler for a reusable resolver and smaller application declarations. The complexity becomes shared; it does not disappear.

Inside Runtime.Dispatch

The adapter above is only the entry point. Here is the shared resolver itself, including the code that reads the mode tables. These are complete functions from the local ochazuke checkout, not pseudocode.

Coverage: the core synchronous dispatch path, not every helper. Bubble Tea delivers a keypress to Model.Update, which adapts it to MacroKey and calls handleKey. The code here then follows Dispatch, dispatchIn, table lookup, runRow, Execute and the scoped action or default handler invocation.

Helper bodies for key classification, guards, argument extraction, context construction and prefix timeout handling are not all shown. The application handler's own work and any off-loop job execution are outside these excerpts.

The runtime still has branches. The difference is ownership. This code implements shared resolution rules once. Application bindings name operations instead of extending a page-by-page keyboard switch.

  1. 1. Dispatch reads the active mode
  2. 2. dispatchIn chooses the matching row
  3. 3. walk and stack determine which contexts participate
  4. 4. lookup gets the mode tables and matches bindings
  5. 5. Noun.tables follows mode inheritance
  6. 6. runRow turns the binding into an operation request
  7. 7. Execute resolves the operation and runs its handler
  8. 8. ActionFor selects the nearest scoped override

1. Dispatch reads the active mode

Dispatch expires a pending sequence, snapshots r.Focus and r.Mode, and substitutes a macro-recording mode when needed. It delegates the actual search to dispatchIn.

2. dispatchIn chooses the matching row

baseAndPrefix separates a sequence mode such as normal g from its base table. Pending and recording modes are exclusive. Capture rows resolve first. The bubbling pass collects the innermost hit, but waits if any eligible level has a longer sequence. A key-class hit stops that scan. An unmatched prefix runs its fallback, then retries the new key.

3. walk and stack determine which contexts participate

walk places capture levels outer-first, then ordinary levels inner-first. stack builds those levels from focus ancestry, restricts them at an active modal, and adds the shared editor fallback only when an input is on the path. Passthrough modes skip capture.

4. lookup gets the mode tables and matches bindings

This is the table lookup. Instance rows come first, then the noun mode and its inherited tables, then the any-mode table if the mode is not exclusive. The matcher filters capture rows and operation applicability, collects exact keys and longer sequences, ranks key-class matches, and applies the binding guard.

5. Noun.tables follows mode inheritance

Bindings are stored in n.Bindings[mode]. Extends points to the parent table. This loop reads the child first and follows the chain, with a cycle check. It does not copy parent rows into the child.

6. runRow turns the binding into an operation request

The selected row supplies its Request. runRow handles pending-mode cleanup, chooses the matched instance as a target when appropriate, fills arguments from the key or mode payload, and calls Execute. Replay rows can dispatch the same key again.

7. Execute resolves the operation and runs its handler

ExecuteAt records history around execute. execute looks up Operations[q.Key()], checks arguments, target and applicability, handles confirmation, then selects a scoped action override or the operation default. This is where a binding finally reaches Go behavior.

8. ActionFor selects the nearest scoped override

The first noun action found along the caller focus ancestry wins. Returning nil tells execute to call op.Run instead.

Define a new action and bind it

  1. Define("app").Verb("pin", handler, description) registers app.pin. The handler toggles state without inspecting a key.
  2. Mode("normal").Bind("p", Do("app.pin")) declares when the operation runs.
  3. Dispatch resolves a keyboard event. Execute invokes the same operation directly.

Observed output / go run / local ochazuke

key: true true <nil> operation: false <nil>

The key is handled and turns the pin on. Direct invocation turns it off. In a TUI, use ochazuke.NewModel(r) for the shared Bubble Tea adapter rather than writing another app-specific keyboard switch.

Real binding tables

The CSV example declares cell and row behavior separately. i and enter call the same operation. y y and d d are sequences, not hand-written prefix branches.

Define a scoped action override

Verb creates an operation when it is new. Action does not register a new operation. It replaces the handler for a registered operation at a noun on the active stack. The core example registers a default first, then gives each noun its own answer.

The conditionals did not vanish. They moved into a reusable resolver and domain handlers. Capture bindings resolve outer-first, then ordinary bindings resolve inner-first. An active modal limits the stack. The first matching row wins. Terminal passthrough modes bypass the capture pass.

Changing a key changes a binding. Changing the operation changes its handler. Context-specific behavior belongs to a scoped action, mode table or named guard, rather than another page branch in the app's keyboard handler.
